channel.title: Raskell - Notes
channel.description: Notes on agent platforms, platform automation, edge infrastructure, and applied security. Building automation-first platforms that survive production reality.

item.title: A capability, democratised
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
Making software used to be reserved for people with a particular privilege: the money to pay a team, or the team itself, or the years it takes to learn to program well enough to build something real. The power I wrote about is that privilege, democratised. Anyone with an idea, a subscription, and the patience to describe what they want can now have it built, and the ones who learn to describe well get a great deal.

Democratised capabilities have a history, and the history has a shape. Nobody who built the printing press or the web could say what people would do with them, and what people did was not on anyone’s plan. The web’s version of that story is in The Web Was the Training Set: a protocol given away, and thirty years of uses nobody at CERN drew. It emerged, from millions of small decisions, and it was better for almost everyone, collectively and in the end, even where it was hard for the people in the middle of it. I expect the same of this, with the same caveat; the move to the city is the comparison I keep returning to. And I expect the window in which it is an advantage rather than a baseline to be short, for the reason in the window before the utility.

item.title: Citizen entrepreneurs
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
A friend of mine, an enterprise architect at a large Swiss energy group, answers the tumult in between with the observation that the same tools that threaten jobs make citizen entrepreneurs possible. An ordinary person can use AI to identify a business opportunity, use AI to build the business, and use AI to operate it. The barrier was never only money; it was the ten different competences a business needs on day one, and those are now available by the hour. The operating half is already true for infrastructure, where one person can now run what used to take a team, as I argued in How AI Makes Bare Metal Viable Again. He took his own idea seriously enough to build a business idea factory, a system that generates and evaluates opportunities. About a week before we talked, someone else announced a project with the same shape on Hacker News, which he took as confirmation rather than competition.

I find it the most hopeful reading of the window, and the one with the most work in it. It assumes the capability really is democratised, which I believe, and it assumes people will take it up, which is the part the window is for.

item.title: Ideas stop waiting
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
I have been shipping more this year than in any year before, and the honest explanation is that nothing changed in me. What changed is that the ideas I had carried in the back of my head for years, project ideas, research questions, things I had never properly put into words, now have a way out. Kishi is one: three game engines and a training loop, which would have been a winter of evenings, done in a month beside a day job. The handbook is another, and what a working day looks like with the agents in it is in How I Work These Days.

I am not faster at the things I already did. A whole category of things has moved from some day to this weekend, and the limiting factor is now how clearly I can say what I want. It feels like a once-in-a-lifetime window, and I think it is one, for a reason I set out in the window before the utility. There is a word for what the window gives a person, and I have come round to it: power, in the good sense.

item.title: Power, in the good sense
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
The word I have settled on for the feeling in ideas stop waiting is power. Not in the sense the word usually carries, power over someone, but in the plain sense: being capable of doing something, having possibilities, having a moat of your own. Through the AI services anyone can subscribe to, we became powerful.

It is an uncomfortable choice of word at first, and the longer I sit with it the more I like it. We have trained ourselves to hear power only as hierarchy, and to look for a victim in every arrangement that has some. This is a kind of power nobody took from anyone. It was not redistributed; it was created, and handed out to whoever cared to learn it. Capability is power, and it is a relief to say so without apology. It is the capability of one person directing many hands, which is what sixteen agents under one manager turned out to be about. What makes it more than a personal feeling is that the capability is democratised, which is where the interesting consequences start.

item.title: The move to the city
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
The comparison I keep coming back to is the move from the land to the city. The industrial cities of the nineteenth century were dense, dirty and short of everything, sanitation first of all; people got sick in them and died in them. The people still on the land did not want to go, and thought life was better where they were, and for them, in their own lifetimes, it often was. Over generations the move made almost everyone better off, and nobody now argues for going back; the long series is on Our World in Data’s page on urbanisation, below.

The thinking today has the same shape. The fear of what AI does to work is legitimate on the timescale of a life, and the long-run reading, that a democratised capability ends up better for everyone collectively, is probably also right. Both can be true, and the part that history does not make comfortable is the middle: the tumult in between.

References

  • Our World in Data, Urbanization: the share of people living in cities over two centuries, by country.

item.title: The tumult in between
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
The two answers people reach for are both answers to the end state. Universal basic income is the money-focused one: if the economy produces enough, pay everyone a floor. Basic access to goods and services is the resource-focused one: if things become nearly free, guarantee the things rather than the money. Each has its advocates and each frightens a lot of people, and neither says anything about the interval. The question is older than AI: Theodor Hertzka’s Freeland and Das soziale Problem, which I have read, are a nineteenth-century design for a society where access to land and capital is guaranteed rather than earned, and the distance between the book and any attempt to live it is the interval I mean.

The interval is the part I cannot see through. If AI really does lead to something like a post-scarcity economy, where most things are virtually free, the jobs go first and the abundance comes later, and in between there is a stretch where people lose their livelihoods at scale with nothing yet in place, and no shared view of where the collective ship is steering. That stretch will be chaotic, and I do not know how long it is. The move to the city says such intervals end well; it does not say they are short. The most constructive response to it I have heard is citizen entrepreneurs.

References

  • Basic Income Earth Network, About basic income: the definition and the main arguments, from the people who have made the case longest.

item.title: The window before the utility
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
I argued in The Economics of Inference that tokens are a metered utility, priced per unit like water or electricity, and that pricing and provision will converge on the utility model. The consequence follows: AI capability will be commoditised. It will become normal, boring, and available to everyone on the same terms, and once it is, having it is no advantage at all, any more than having electricity is. The model behind it becomes a dependency like any other, the argument of The Model Is a Dependency, and its bill gets metered into the loop, as in The Bill Is Part of the Loop.

That is the end state. We are not there. The models, the tools and the prices are still moving every quarter, and in a moving market the advantage goes to the people who adopt early and learn to use the thing well, which is work. This is why the feeling in ideas stop waiting is a window and not a new normal: nobody in 2036 will write a note about feeling empowered by their electricity supply. The window is open now, it is once in a lifetime in the literal sense, and what one does with it is the question. One answer is in citizen entrepreneurs.

item.title: Opus 5.5 is the best Opus since 4.5
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
Opus 4.5Opus 5.5
Released24 November 202522 September 2026
Price per million tokens, input / output$5 / $25$4 / $20
Fast modenot offered$8 / $40
Context window200K1M
Model IDclaude-opus-4-5-20251101claude-opus-5-5

Opus 4.5 was the moment Claude Code started working the way it was meant to. I had paid for Claude Code since May 2025 without being convinced; over the 2025 Christmas break, with Opus 4.5, it carried whole projects, and I built Zentinel with it. I wrote that up in How I Work These Days and What Sixteen AI Agents Taught Me About Management, and it is the opening of my Basel talk.

Opus 5.5 is the first release since then that felt like the same kind of step rather than an increment.

  • It holds the thread. Long sessions that span a theme, a site, CI, and several data files stay coherent. The search across this site, the reading log, and the agent-readable files behind them were built in sessions with it.
  • Speed changes how I work with it. Fast enough that I stay in the loop instead of switching away while it runs. Fast mode exists for when that matters more than the bill.
  • The cost moved the right way. A cheaper rate card than 4.5, and Anthropic puts it at about 40 per cent cheaper to run than Opus 5 on typical work. The rate card is half the story; fewer wasted turns is the other half, the same argument I made in The Economics of Inference.
  • Opus is the default again. For most of my work I no longer pick a smaller model to save money, which was the point of 4.5 too.

What I do not know yet: whether it holds up on the hardest, longest-running tasks, where the gap to a larger model would show first. A month is not a benchmark.

Sources: Introducing Claude Opus 4.5, Introducing Claude Opus 5.5, Opus 5.5 model overview.
